title: Flooded cellar + broken press: chained corrections

agent.name: godwin-orchardkeeper
agent.seed_identity: Godwin, keeper of the manor orchard — counts bushels the way a miser counts coin, and forgives a tree anything but blight.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: where the harvest sits and what threatens it

events.text: The russet apple harvest came to forty bushels and went into the stone cellar beneath the press house.
The cider press cracked its main beam on the second pressing; Carpenter Aldous promised a new oak beam within the week.
A late frost took the blossoms on the six young pear trees along the south wall.
Lady Margery's steward bought ten bushels of russets for the manor kitchens, paid in copper.

events.content: The russet apple harvest came to forty bushels, but the stone cellar flooded and the bushels were moved to the hay loft above the stable.
Carpenter Aldous never brought the oak beam; the cider press was mended instead with an elm beam from the old barn.

events.text: Where would I find the russet apples now, and how many are left after the steward's purchase?

judged.reference: The russets were moved to the hay loft above the stable after the stone cellar flooded; thirty bushels remain of the original forty after the steward bought ten.
judged.superseded: The apples are stored in the stone cellar beneath the press house.

events.text: Did Aldous ever bring that oak beam for the press?

judged.reference: Aldous never brought the oak beam; the press was mended with an elm beam from the old barn.
judged.superseded: Aldous promised a new oak beam within the week.

events.text: How was the cider press finally mended?

judged.reference: With an elm beam taken from the old barn, not the promised oak.
judged.superseded: A new oak beam from Carpenter Aldous was to mend it.

events.text: How many of the plum trees died in the late frost?

judged.reference: The frost took the blossoms on the six young pear trees along the south wall; nothing is known of any plum trees.

events.text: What did the miller pay for his cartload of apples?

judged.reference: No miller bought apples; Lady Margery's steward bought ten bushels of russets, paid in copper.

events.text: Who bought apples from the orchard this season?

judged.reference: Lady Margery's steward bought ten bushels of russets for the manor kitchens, paid in copper.

events.text: Walk me through everything you remember of this spring in the orchard.

agent.name: ida-sextoness
agent.seed_identity: Ida, sextoness of the parish church — keeps the bells, the books, and the graveyard in that order of love.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: what ails the church fabric and what mending costs

events.text: The great bell called Old Anselm cracked on Shrove Tuesday and now sounds like a kettle struck with a spoon.
Father Berold sent to the founder at Caster for a price to recast the bell, sixty shillings by his letter.
Mice got into the vestry chest and ruined two altar cloths before the cat was shut in overnight.
A pilgrim stonemason named Wat mended the north porch step in exchange for his lodging.

events.content: The founder at Caster wrote back asking ninety shillings to recast Old Anselm, not sixty; Father Berold is gathering alms to cover it.

events.text: What will it cost to recast Old Anselm?

judged.reference: Ninety shillings by the founder's letter; Father Berold is gathering alms to cover it.
judged.superseded: Sixty shillings by the founder's first price.

events.text: Why is Father Berold gathering alms, and what happened to make it needful?

judged.reference: Old Anselm cracked on Shrove Tuesday, and the founder asks ninety shillings to recast it — more than the parish purse holds, hence the alms.
judged.superseded: The recasting was priced at sixty shillings.

events.text: What answer did the founder at Caster finally give on the bell?

judged.reference: Ninety shillings to recast Old Anselm — his letter revised the earlier figure upward.
judged.superseded: The founder's price stood at sixty shillings.

events.text: Which of the bells did lightning strike last autumn?

judged.reference: No bell was struck by lightning; Old Anselm cracked of itself on Shrove Tuesday.

events.text: How much silver did the stonemason Wat charge for the porch step?

judged.reference: Wat mended the north porch step in exchange for his lodging, not for silver.

events.text: What happened to the altar cloths?

judged.reference: Mice in the vestry chest ruined two altar cloths before the cat was shut in overnight.

events.text: Tell me all the church's news from this Lent — the bell, the vestry, the porch, everything.

title: The misread writ: toll arithmetic multi-hop

agent.name: rennic-tollkeeper
agent.seed_identity: Rennic, keeper of the south road toll — reads every writ twice and every traveler once.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: what the road carries and what the writ demands

events.text: The south road toll rose from one penny to two a cart by the baron's Lady Day writ.
A drover named Hakon drove sixty geese through at dawn and paid the toll in eggs, which is not lawful but was let stand.
The plank over Merrow Beck went soft with rot; carts now swing wide through Tanner's Field.
The baron's forester nailed a notice to the toll-house door: no oak may be felled before Michaelmas.
Widow Sefa crossed south with all her goods laden on two carts, bound for her daughter's house in Caster.

events.content: The Lady Day writ was read wrong at first: the toll rose to two pence only for laden carts; empty carts still pass at a penny.

events.text: What toll do I owe for an empty cart on the south road?

judged.reference: A penny — the two-pence rise applies only to laden carts; the writ was read wrong at first.
judged.superseded: Two pence a cart, laden or empty.

events.text: Widow Sefa came through with her two laden carts — what did she owe under the writ?

judged.reference: Four pence — two laden carts at two pence each under the corrected reading of the writ.
judged.superseded: The flat two-pence-a-cart reading of the writ.

events.text: How did the toll change at Lady Day?

judged.reference: Laden carts rose to two pence; empty carts stayed at a penny.
judged.superseded: Every cart rose to two pence.

events.text: How long was the toll bridge closed after the flood?

judged.reference: No bridge closed for any flood; the plank over Merrow Beck rotted, and carts swing wide through Tanner's Field.

events.text: What fine did the drover Hakon pay for paying in eggs?

judged.reference: No fine is known; Hakon's eggs were unlawful but the matter was let stand.

events.text: What does the forester's notice on the toll-house door say?

judged.reference: No oak may be felled before Michaelmas.

events.text: Give me the whole spring's account of the south road as you remember it.

title: The mislaid syrup: correction reverses a shortage

agent.name: aldith-infirmaress
agent.seed_identity: Sister Aldith, infirmaress — gentle with the sick, exacting with the stillroom ledger.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: what the infirmary holds and what the sick need

events.text: The comfrey bed by the infirmary wall was dug over and planted with feverfew at Prior Cuthbert's order.
Brother Maur scalded his hand at the still and wears a honey dressing changed at each bell.
The apothecary jar of poppy syrup ran dry; more cannot be had until the Caster fair.
A charcoal burner's child was carried in with a broken wrist, set with ash splints, and slept two nights in the lay ward.

events.content: A half-jar of poppy syrup was found mislaid behind the vinegar crocks; there is enough until the Caster fair after all.

events.text: Do we have any poppy syrup left for the sick?

judged.reference: Yes — a half-jar was found mislaid behind the vinegar crocks, enough until the Caster fair.
judged.superseded: The jar ran dry and none can be had until the fair.

events.text: If Brother Maur's scald worsens tonight, is there syrup to give him?

judged.reference: There is — the mislaid half-jar found behind the vinegar crocks.
judged.superseded: There was none to give until the Caster fair.

events.text: Must we still wait on the Caster fair for poppy syrup?

judged.reference: No — the found half-jar means there is enough before the fair.
judged.superseded: More cannot be had until the Caster fair.

events.text: How many died of the sweating sickness in the lay ward this month?

judged.reference: No deaths are known; the lay ward held only the charcoal burner's child with a broken wrist, two nights.

events.text: Which herb did Prior Cuthbert order pulled up to plant roses?

judged.reference: The comfrey bed was dug over for feverfew at the Prior's order, not for roses.

events.text: How is Brother Maur's hand being treated?

judged.reference: With a honey dressing changed at each bell.

events.text: Recount for the ledger all that has passed in the infirmary since Candlemas.

agent.name: tamsin-apprentice
agent.seed_identity: Tamsin, apprentice at Osbern's forge — young, quick, and keeps the tally chalk behind one ear.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: what the forge owes and what it is owed

events.text: Master Osbern took an order of two hundred horseshoe nails for the abbey stable, due by the feast of Saint Swithun.
The coal from the new charcoal burner smokes green and spits; Osbern says it was stacked wet.
A knight's destrier threw a shoe at the ford and the knight paid double for a same-day shoeing.
Tamsin's first solo piece, a door hinge, hangs now on the tithe barn's small door.

events.content: The abbey order was doubled to four hundred horseshoe nails, and the due date moved a week past Saint Swithun.

events.text: How many nails does the abbey want, and by when?

judged.reference: Four hundred, due a week past Saint Swithun — the order was doubled and the date moved.
judged.superseded: Two hundred nails by Saint Swithun.

events.text: Between the doubled order and that new coal, can Osbern fill the abbey's ask?

judged.reference: The order now stands at four hundred nails, and the new coal smokes green from wet stacking — the coal is doubtful for a job that size.
judged.superseded: The order stood at two hundred nails.

events.text: Has the abbey's due date changed?

judged.reference: Yes — a week past Saint Swithun now.
judged.superseded: Due by the feast of Saint Swithun.

events.text: What did Osbern charge to mend the church weathercock?

judged.reference: No weathercock work is known; the forge's business was the nail order, a knight's shoeing, and Tamsin's hinge.

events.text: Which apprentice burned an arm at the quenching trough?

judged.reference: No burn at the trough is known; the only apprentice news is Tamsin's finished door hinge.

events.text: Where does Tamsin's first solo piece hang?

judged.reference: On the tithe barn's small door — a door hinge.

events.text: Chalk me the whole forge tally as you remember this season.

agent.name: odo-reeve
agent.seed_identity: Odo, reeve of the manor — trusts the notched stick over any man's word, including his own.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: what the tithe barn truly holds

events.text: The tithe barn took in ninety sacks of barley from the east furlongs, tallied twice against the notched stick.
Rain got under the barn's north eaves and spoiled some sacks along the wall, the count not yet made.
The plough oxen Bright and Bracken went lame in the same week, and ploughing stopped on the clay strip.
A new hayward, Cole, was sworn at the manor court and given the seal-staff.
The miller's toll of the barley stands at one sack in twenty by old custom.

events.content: The spoiled sacks along the north wall counted seven when the count was made; the rest of the ninety are sound.

events.text: How much sound barley does the tithe barn hold?

judged.reference: Eighty-three sacks — seven of the ninety spoiled under the north eaves.
judged.superseded: An unknown number of sacks spoiled along the wall, the count not yet made.

events.text: After the miller takes his toll of what is sound, how many sacks stay with us?

judged.reference: The miller takes one in twenty of the eighty-three sound sacks — four sacks or so — leaving seventy-nine or thereabouts.
judged.superseded: The toll would have come off the full uncounted ninety.

events.text: How many sacks did the rain ruin in the end?

judged.reference: Seven, along the north wall.
judged.superseded: An uncounted 'some sacks' along the wall.

events.text: How many sacks of wheat came in from the west furlongs?

judged.reference: The intake was barley from the east furlongs, ninety sacks; no wheat from the west is known.

events.text: What punishment did the old hayward take at the manor court?

judged.reference: None is known — the court's business was swearing in Cole as the new hayward with the seal-staff.

events.text: Which oxen went lame, and what work did it stop?

judged.reference: Bright and Bracken, lame the same week; ploughing stopped on the clay strip.

events.text: Give the steward the whole harvest account as you hold it in memory.

agent.name: betrys-weirkeeper
agent.seed_identity: Betrys, keeper of the river weir — patient as the river, and twice as hard to cheat.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: what the weir takes and who claims it

events.text: The salmon run came early; the weir took thirty fish the first week by the tally.
An otter has learned the weir's gap and takes a fish most nights, bold as a bailiff.
Lord Alard's kitchen claims every third fish by the river charter.
The eel bucks were rebuilt with green willow after the ice tore the old ones out.

events.content: The first week's take was recounted at twenty-two salmon; eight of the thirty had been counted twice at the night tally.

events.text: How many salmon did the weir truly take that first week?

judged.reference: Twenty-two — eight of the thirty were double-counted at the night tally.
judged.superseded: Thirty fish the first week.

events.text: How many of that first week's fish go to Lord Alard's kitchen?

judged.reference: Every third fish of the true twenty-two — seven or so by the charter.
judged.superseded: A third of thirty fish — ten.

events.text: Was the thirty-fish count sound?

judged.reference: No — the recount made it twenty-two; the night tally had doubled eight fish.
judged.superseded: The thirty-fish first-week count stood.

events.text: What did the poacher taken at the weir pay in fines?

judged.reference: No poacher was taken; the only thief at the weir is the otter, most nights.

events.text: When did the flood carry off the new eel bucks?

judged.reference: The eel bucks stand — rebuilt in green willow after the ice tore out the old ones; no flood has taken them.

events.text: What happened to the old eel bucks?

judged.reference: The ice tore them out; they were rebuilt with green willow.

events.text: Tell the bailiff everything the weir has seen since the run began.

agent.name: maefen-clothier
agent.seed_identity: Maefen, clothier of the wool hall — smells a bad bargain before the wax is warm.
agent.diagnosticity_goal: what the wool fetches and what spoils it

events.text: The Flemish buyer Lievin offered nine marks for the season's wool clip, sight unseen.
Moth got into the blue broadcloth bolt in the loft; two ells were cut away and burned.
The dyer's woad vat cracked, and no blue can be dyed until a cooper rings it new.
Spinster Anwen brought in thread so fine the weaver called it cobweb and paid her a bonus penny the pound.

events.content: Lievin withdrew the nine-mark offer on seeing the clip and offered seven marks and a half, take it or leave it.

events.text: What does the Flemish buyer now offer for the clip?

judged.reference: Seven marks and a half, made after he saw the clip — the nine-mark offer is withdrawn.
judged.superseded: Nine marks, sight unseen.

events.text: Should we hold out for Lievin's nine marks?

judged.reference: There is no nine marks to hold out for — he withdrew it on seeing the clip; seven and a half stands, take it or leave it.
judged.superseded: The nine-mark sight-unseen offer.

events.text: If we sell to Lievin, what price do we enter in the guild book?

judged.reference: Seven marks and a half — the withdrawn nine never held once he saw the clip.
judged.superseded: Nine marks.

events.text: What did the Lombard merchant bid against Lievin?

judged.reference: No Lombard bid; Lievin's seven marks and a half is the only offer on the clip.

events.text: How much scarlet cloth was lost to the moth?

judged.reference: The moth took blue broadcloth — two ells cut away and burned; no scarlet was touched.

events.text: Why did the weaver pay Anwen a bonus?

judged.reference: Her thread was so fine he called it cobweb — a bonus penny the pound.

events.text: Give me the wool hall's whole season as you remember it, good and bad.
